# LLM multi-agent simulations of market events do not give reproducible readings at 7B scale

**Status:** negative result, complete and self-contained.
**Date:** 2026-08-02.
**Hardware:** one consumer GPU, 8 GB VRAM (RTX 5060 Laptop).
**Model:** `qwen2.5:7b-instruct` via Ollama.
**Simulator:** MiroFish-Offline (multi-agent, Neo4j-backed), patched for deterministic cohort construction.

---

## Update — v1.1 (2026-08-05)

**v1.0 is unchanged and still tagged.** This section adds what a further four
days of measurement found. Two of v1.0's statements need correcting and one of
its central numbers no longer stands.

### Temperature 0 bites at only one of three layers

v1.0 set four cohort-construction temperatures to 0 and deliberately left the
interview layer stochastic. Measuring each layer separately:

| layer | temperature | deterministic? |
|---|---|---|
| entity extraction | 0 | **no** — two builds of one input in one container gave 27 and 26 entities, 24 shared |
| persona generation | 0 | **no** — on a *fixed* `graph_id`, two `prepare` calls gave `persona` differing 20/20 |
| interview | 0 | **yes** — eight rounds byte-identical within one simulation |
| interview | default | no — worst-of-4 D₂ = 0.2121 over eight rounds |

So "we determinised cohort construction" was true of the setting and false of the
effect. Setting the temperature to 0 did not make those two layers deterministic.

### Correction 1 — "byte-identical rosters" was a hash of names only

v1.0 reports that runs 2, 3 and 4 had byte-identical rosters, from a sha256 of
persona *names* with the random numeric suffix stripped. Comparing the full
profiles instead:

| pair | `persona` differs | reading D₂ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 vs 2 / 3 / 4 | 19/19 | 0.5877 / 0.3165 / 0.5572 |
| 2 vs 3 | 3/20 | 0.2828 |
| 2 vs 4 | 3/20 | **0.0393** |
| 3 vs 4 | **0/20** | 0.2481 |

Only one pair had identical personas. And the relationship is not monotone at
n=4: the pair with identical people differs by 0.2481 in the final reading, while
the closest reading pair had three personas differing. **Identical names do not
imply identical people, and identical people did not produce identical readings.**

### Correction 2 — the roster contains entities that are not people

Entity extraction emits sentence fragments, and they are promoted to personas. A
roster of twenty contained `market event` and **`MiroFish`** — the simulator's own
name — as two of the twenty "people". They were interviewed and they answered,
and their answers entered every figure in v1.0. Reported upstream as
[666ghj/MiroFish#759](https://github.com/666ghj/MiroFish/issues/759).

### Correction 3 — the k = 206 cost figure should not have been quoted

v1.0 derived "206 runs, about 48 hours per event" from a worst-of-4 statistic
over four samples. `worst_of_4` is an extreme-value statistic, not a σ, and the
six pairwise distances span fifteen-fold (0.0393 to 0.5877). Depending on the
estimator, k comes out as 1, 54, 69 or 206. **No single k is credible.**

The conclusion survives because it does not depend on the estimator: at k = 25 —
more optimistic than any measurement here — a 25-event study still needs 229
hours of continuous machine time; at k = 206 it needs 1888. Ten days against
seventy-nine. Infeasible either way, which is what v1.0 concluded, for a reason
that now reads differently: **not because k is large, but because the repetition
unit can only be the simulation.**

### Three ways to pin the cohort, all closed

| attempt | result |
|---|---|
| freeze the temperatures | extraction and persona generation remain nondeterministic |
| freeze the graph | same `graph_id`, `persona` still 20/20 different |
| freeze `reddit_profiles.json` and skip `prepare` | pipeline refuses: `Simulation not ready. Current status: created. Please call /prepare first` |

Registered before the last attempt: if it failed, the conclusion settles and no
fourth workaround would be tried. It failed.

**One natural experiment says the fix would work if it were available.** Runs 3
and 4 came from different simulations yet produced identical personas, and their
reading distance (0.2481) falls back to the within-simulation scale (0.2121)
rather than the 0.32–0.59 seen when personas differ. This is an n=1 pairing
between two different estimators and nothing is computed from it — but pinning
the cohort evidently helps, and none of the three ways of pinning it is open from
outside the simulator.

### What v1.0 got right and what changed

Right: readings of the same input are not reproducible at this scale, and the
hypothesis about second-order reasoning remains untested rather than refuted.

Changed: the reason. v1.0 attributed the residual variance to the interview layer
after "determinising the cohort". The cohort was never determinised — the setting
was applied, the effect was not — and the variance is dominated by a cohort that
is rebuilt differently every time.

## 中文摘要

**在消费级硬件上、在 7B 规模上**（8 GB 显存、`qwen2.5:7b-instruct`），
LLM 多智能体模拟对单个金融事件产出的方向读数**不可复现**。
本结论只针对这一个具体配置——它比「多智能体模拟不行」窄得多，而窄正是它的价值所在。同一份输入、同一套问卷：

- 四次运行 P(up) 落在 **0.312 – 0.768**（其中首次方向相反，但该次人群少一个实体，不完全可比）
- **即使排除首次运行**，余下三次**人群花名册逐位相同**，P(up) 仍摆 **0.568 – 0.768**

后者才是最干净的证据，且已足够。

而**同一基座上的单次提问基线（方法 A）在同样两份 packet 上各 60 次调用、方向 100% 一致**
（E1 全 down、E4 全 up——说明它确实在读 packet，不是在输出常量）。
在同一把尺子下（两臂都按置信度加权），A 的 `worst4` = **0.041**，B = **0.382**，
**差约一个数量级**。这与「不稳定性属于管线而非 7B 基座」一致，但该判据是**压线**通过的
（余量 2.3×10⁻⁵，小于度量本身的量化步长），故记作**描述性观察，而非判据支持的判定**。

因此在该配置下**无法检验**「多智能体二阶推演是否带来增量信息」这一假设。
**不是假设被证伪，是仪器达不到可测量的精度。**

关键在于这是**受控**的：我们先把人群构建确定化（四次中三次花名册逐位相同），
从而排除了最容易被归咎的解释——「每次的人群不一样」。方差在那之后依然存在。

本结论**不依赖任何真实市场结果**，判定量按构造就不需要它。

---

## Why this is worth writing down

A large number of projects currently run agent-population simulations on 7B/8B
local models and report conclusions of the form "the simulation shows...".
Almost none report run-to-run variance of the same input.

We measured it, under a controlled condition that rules out the explanation most
people would reach for first — that the crowd differs between runs. It does not.
The variance survives a byte-identical crowd.

The result also sidesteps every contamination problem that dogged the rest of
this project: it never touches a market outcome, so blinding failures, selection
effects, and label-timing issues cannot reach it.

---

## Setup

**Task.** A "packet" describes a breaking market event at time T0: up to 12
headlines from distinct outlets in the preceding 24h, the prediction target
symbol, a T0 price snapshot, an optional prediction-market line, and a forecast
horizon. The simulation ingests the packet, builds a population of personas from
it, runs a social simulation, then interviews each persona for a directional
expectation over the horizon.

**The reading.** Each persona answers on a −2..+2 scale (clearly lower →
clearly higher). Personas answering 0 are counted as abstaining. The crowd is
mapped to a probability vector over (up, down, flat) by

```
p = w · vote_distribution + (1 − w) · base_rate
w = (# personas with a non-zero answer) / (# personas)
base_rate = (0.365, 0.365, 0.27)
```

The shrinkage toward the base rate is what keeps a near-silent crowd from
producing a confident-looking reading.

**Distance between two readings.** `D₂ = ‖p₁ − p₂‖₂`. This needs no outcome; it
compares two readings of the same input to each other. We also report
`maxⱼ |Brier(p₁,j) − Brier(p₂,j)|` — the worst case over the three possible
outcomes, which likewise depends only on p₁ and p₂ — but it decides nothing.

---

## The determinisation step (what makes this controlled)

Repeating the same packet initially produced a **different crowd every time**:
new ontology, new entities, new personas. On one packet, a byte-identical
interview prompt gave 9.5% and 60.0% abstention on two runs.

Two design choices were tangled together:

1. the crowd should be **derived from the event** — the simulator's whole point;
2. the crowd should be **re-randomised on every rerun** — no reason at all.

A full audit of `temperature=` across the simulator's backend found 12 sites.
Tracing reachability from the five endpoints this project calls identified
**four** on the cohort-construction path:

| file | reached via |
|---|---|
| `ontology_generator.py` | `POST /api/graph/ontology/generate` |
| `ner_extractor.py` | `POST /api/graph/build` |
| `oasis_profile_generator.py` | `POST /api/simulation/prepare` |
| `simulation_config_generator.py` | `SimulationManager.prepare_simulation()` |

All four set to 0. Sites in the report-generation and graph-query paths were left
alone (never called here), and **the interview stage was deliberately left
stochastic** — per-agent response variation is the phenomenon under study, not
noise to be removed.

Two notes for anyone repeating this:

* Both retry ladders were **descending** (`0.7 − attempt·0.1`, for more reliable
  JSON on retry), not ascending escape hatches. A flat 0 is therefore both
  deterministic and the most reliable setting; keeping the ladder with base 0
  would compute negative temperatures.
* The simulator's compose files use `build: .` and mount only an uploads
  directory, so **editing host source changes nothing until the image is
  rebuilt**. We verify the effective temperatures *inside the running container*
  before every run, and the run refuses to start if they are not 0 — including
  when the check itself cannot run.

---

## Result

Four runs, same packet, same frozen questionnaire, patched image, temperature
gate passed before each:

| # | personas | with a view | abstention | w | P(up) | P(down) | P(flat) | wall clock | peak VRAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 19 | 11 | 42.1% | 0.579 | **0.312** | 0.575 | 0.114 | 12.0 min | 6509 MB |
| 2 | 20 | 19 | 5.0% | 0.950 | **0.768** | 0.218 | 0.014 | 14.3 min | 6479 MB |
| 3 | 20 | 19 | 5.0% | 0.950 | **0.568** | 0.418 | 0.014 | 14.8 min | 6136 MB |
| 4 | 20 | 20 | 0.0% | 1.000 | **0.750** | 0.250 | 0.000 | 15.7 min | 6142 MB |

Zero parse failures (0/19, 0/20, 0/20, 0/20). Zero errors. VRAM by `nvidia-smi`.

Pairwise distances:

| pair | D₂ | worst-case Brier gap |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | **0.5879** | 0.9107 |
| 1–3 | 0.3169 | 0.4556 |
| 1–4 | 0.5573 | 0.8341 |
| 2–3 | 0.2828 | 0.5400 |
| 2–4 | 0.0390 | 0.0765 |
| 3–4 | 0.2480 | 0.4635 |

**P(up) ranges from 0.312 to 0.768. Run 1 points the opposite way from the
other three.** Excluding run 1 — the only one whose roster differs — the three
byte-identical-roster runs still range 0.568 to 0.768.

### The shrinkage term moves too, and it *narrows* the reported spread

`w` is not constant across runs: 0.579, 0.950, 0.950, 1.000. So P(up) moves for
two reasons at once — the vote split changes, and the strength of the shrinkage
toward the base rate changes with it. Anyone reusing this mapping will hit that.

Inverting the shrinkage to recover the raw vote split:

| run | w | P(up) after shrinkage | raw share voting up |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.579 | 0.312 | **0.273** |
| 2 | 0.950 | 0.768 | **0.789** |
| 3 | 0.950 | 0.568 | **0.579** |
| 4 | 1.000 | 0.750 | **0.750** |

The raw split ranges **51.6pp** (0.273–0.789); after shrinkage the reported
figure ranges **45.6pp**. The shrinkage *compressed* the disagreement — run 1's
low `w` pulled it toward the base rate and toward the others. **The headline
45.6pp therefore understates crowd-level disagreement, it does not inflate it.**

### The crowd really was identical

Comparing `reddit_profiles.json` across the four runs, stripping the random
numeric suffix appended to usernames:

| run | personas | roster sha256 (first 12) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 19 | `8c585d217d02` |
| 2 | 20 | **`90caa587f7cb`** |
| 3 | 20 | **`90caa587f7cb`** |
| 4 | 20 | **`90caa587f7cb`** |

Runs 2, 3 and 4 have **byte-identical rosters**. Run 1 differs by a single
missing entity (`market_event`) on the first run after container start. The
persona names recur exactly across runs — only the random numeric suffix moves.

So: **the determinisation worked.** And with a byte-identical crowd, the same
packet and the same questions, runs 2 and 3 produce the *same* 5.0% abstention
and P(up) of **0.768 vs 0.568**.

The residual variance is in the interview stage — in how a persona answers, not
in which personas exist.

---

## What this does and does not say

**It says:** at this scale, a single-event reading from this pipeline is not
reproducible at the precision any downstream comparison would need. Not "the
signal is weak" — the same input does not yield the same number twice.

**It does not say** that the underlying hypothesis (that multi-agent second-order
reasoning adds information over a single-shot baseline) is false. Nothing here
touched a market outcome. The hypothesis is untested, not refuted.

**It does not say** that averaging cannot rescue it. Under the pre-registered
criterion, worst-pair D₂ = 0.5879 against a 0.041 threshold implies
`k = ceil((0.5879/0.041)²) = 206` runs per event — about 48 hours of compute for
one event. But that formula assumes the runs are independent draws around a
stable centre, and **four runs cannot test that assumption**. The four P(up)
values average 0.5995; a distribution centred near 0.60 with SD ≈ 0.2 would
produce exactly this sample. So k = 206 should be read as "the extrapolation is
not credible", not as a price list.

Worth noting: a centre near 0.60 against a 0.365 base rate is itself suspicious.
This project separately recorded a cross-event pattern of uniform optimism from
this model ("financial-advisor optimism"). If a stable centre exists, it may be
the model's baseline disposition rather than event information.

---

## Limitations

1. **n = 4.** Enough to show the spread is large; not enough to characterise its
   distribution, and specifically not enough to distinguish "wide noise around a
   stable centre" from "no stable centre".
2. **One packet, one event type.** The four runs share a single packet (a chip /
   tech event). Variance on other event types is unmeasured.
3. **One model, one quantisation.** `qwen2.5:7b-instruct`. The A-arm experiment
   below is *consistent with* the instability being pipeline-specific rather than
   a base-model property, but it lands on the decision threshold rather than
   clearing it, so it is a descriptive observation and not a verdict. Whether a
   larger model would change the pipeline's behaviour is untested.
4. **`q1_position == 0` is counted as abstention**, so the vote distribution
   carries mass on up/down only and `P(flat)` is always exactly `(1−w)·0.27`.
   The method structurally cannot express a flat expectation beyond the base
   rate, and it conflates "no view" with "expects no move". This was left
   unchanged because the instrument's calibration was measured under it.
5. **The 9.3× gap is a lower bound, not an estimate.** Correcting A's metric
   narrowed but did not remove the resolution asymmetry. A still emits 3 calls
   whose probabilities take only a handful of values, so its `D₂` remains
   quantised — {0, 0.0205, 0.041, 0.0615, 0.082, 0.123} on this data. B, over 20
   personas with continuously varying `w` and vote split, is effectively
   continuous. Comparing the dispersion of a quantised quantity to a continuous
   one still favours the quantised one. We stopped correcting here deliberately:
   the asymmetry is now small enough that it does not change the direction of the
   result, and chasing it further has no natural end point. **Read 9.3× as "at
   least 9.3×".**
6. **Run 1 is not fully comparable** — 19 personas rather than 20, on the first
   run after a container restart. Excluding it, worst-pair D₂ among the three
   byte-identical-roster runs is still 0.2828, ~7× the threshold.

---

## Is it the model or the pipeline?

*(A-arm experiment — see `protocol/instrument-selection-rule.md` appendix T16-0
for the pre-registered criteria, and the section below for results.)*

The obvious next question is whether this instability belongs to the 7B base
model — in which case any multi-sample aggregation on it is equally affected and
a larger model is the only route — or to the multi-agent pipeline specifically,
in which case model size is unlikely to help.

The discriminating experiment is cheap: run the single-shot baseline (method A)
many times on the same packet and compare its dispersion.

Two asymmetries in that comparison both push toward the "base model" verdict and
must be handled, or the experiment silently recommends buying a bigger model:

* **Pair count.** A worst-pair over 190 pairs exceeds a worst-pair over 6 by
  construction. Measured on a synthetic sample from one distribution: 190-pair
  max 0.9916 vs equal-count worst-of-4 median 0.5469 — a 1.8× inflation. We
  therefore compare a median worst-of-4 from 2000 random 4-subsets.
* **Aggregation width.** A aggregates 3 samples; B aggregates 20. Fewer samples
  disperse more. This is *not* corrected; instead the evidence bar is
  asymmetric — "A is steadier" is strong (it wins despite the handicap),
  "A is noisier" is weak and is labelled as such.

### The first version of this comparison was broken

The direction-only mapping is **degenerate for arm A**, and the first version of
this section did not notice. Stated plainly because it nearly produced a wrong
conclusion:

* A emits one direction plus a confidence. The mapping reads direction only.
* A's 3 calls have 27 possible direction combinations, which the mapping
  collapses onto just **10** distinct vectors. B, over 20 personas with a
  continuously varying `w`, ranges over ~**231**.
* When A's 3 calls agree on direction, `p` is **exactly** `(1,0,0)` or `(0,1,0)`
  — *independent of the confidence*.
* **All 40 A runs were unanimous.** So `A_worst4 = 0.0000` was an algebraic
  identity, not a measurement. The two arms were on rulers differing 23× in
  resolution.

**Correction.** `probability` is confidence in the stated direction, so each
reading maps to a vector with `q` on that direction and the remaining `1−q` split
across the other two classes in proportion to their base rates — no new
parameter. Applied to A only: B's mapping is frozen and the k decision rests on
it. This correction is **post-hoc**, and its approximate magnitude was known
before it was computed; it is not credited as a rule written before the data.

### Result

20 repetitions of method A (3 internal calls each, 60 calls per packet):

| packet | directions (60 calls) | `A_worst4` direction-only | `A_worst4` corrected | B |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 (chip/tech) | **`down` × 60** | 0.0000 *(degenerate)* | **0.040977** | 0.5879 |
| E4 | **`up` × 60** | 0.0000 *(degenerate)* | **0.040977** | — |

**A gives opposite directions on the two packets** — *down* on E1, *up* on E4 —
so its reproducibility is not a constant-output artefact. A reads the packet, and
reads it the same way every time.

#### The threshold result is on a knife edge and must not be read as a verdict

`A_worst4 = 0.040977` against a threshold of `0.041`. It passes **by
2.3 × 10⁻⁵**.

That margin is meaningless. A's probabilities take only the values
{60, 70, 75, 80}, so `D₂` can only take
{0, 0.0205, 0.041, 0.0615, 0.082, 0.123} — and the threshold happens to sit
between two adjacent achievable values, with the median worst-of-4 landing
exactly on the one below. **One more run differing by a single 10pp step could
flip the verdict.**

So, both readings, plainly:

* **Literal application of the pre-registered rule:** `≤ 0.041` → "pipeline
  property, strong branch". It passes.
* **Honest reading:** the margin is four orders of magnitude below the metric's
  own quantisation step. This is a boundary, not a pass. **The claim is therefore
  demoted from a criterion-backed verdict to a descriptive observation**, and the
  pre-registered bands were *not* redrawn to avoid that demotion.

#### The substantive comparison

| | `worst4` | ratio vs A |
|---|---|---|
| A, confidence-weighted | **0.0410** | — |
| B, frozen mapping (the k decision) | **0.5879** | **14.3×** |
| B, confidence-weighted *(descriptive only)* | **0.3822** | **9.3×** |

The last row is the fairest single comparison — both arms on the same ruler. A
prediction made when this check was pre-registered was **wrong**: we expected
weighting B by its `q2_conviction` to *increase* B's dispersion, making the
A-only correction conservative. It *decreased* it, 0.5879 → 0.3822. The gap
narrows from 14.3× to 9.3×; the direction is unchanged.

**Descriptive conclusion:** on the same ruler, the single-shot baseline is roughly
an order of magnitude more reproducible than the multi-agent pipeline on the same
packets. That is consistent with the instability being pipeline-specific rather
than a property of the 7B base model — but on this evidence it is an observation,
not a criterion the data passed.

### What this implies

The variance enters somewhere between "one model call on the packet" and "twenty
personas answering in character, aggregated". Candidates, none tested here:
persona role-play amplifying sampling entropy; the social-simulation rounds
compounding it; the aggregation being computed over too few effective voters
once abstention is counted. Aggregating 20 personas visibly does **not** average
the noise away — it produces more spread than 3 plain samples.

That is a pipeline-design problem, and it is a more tractable one than "buy a
bigger GPU".

---

## About this repository's history

The full development history is retained deliberately: `protocol/` and the
section below cite **13 commit hashes**, and the claim that each rule was
committed *before* the data it governs is only checkable if those hashes resolve.
A fresh `git init` would break every one of them, which would turn the single
strongest checkable claim here into a false statement.

The cost is that the history contains material outside this result, stated here
rather than left to be discovered:

* **`p2/`** — infrastructure for a forward-validation study (event trigger,
  append-only ledger, settlement) that this finding does not draw on.
* **`results/` and one round of blind grading** — **voided**. Its blinding failed:
  all three graders identified the arms correctly, so the grades cannot be
  treated as blind. Recorded in `protocol/CHANGELOG.md` under 2026-07-27 and
  2026-07-28, including the arithmetic corrections that followed.
* **Early revisions carry the author's local paths** (`D:\...` in two commits).
  Cleaned from the working tree, not rewritten in history — rewriting would
  change the hashes above.

All of it is removed from the working tree in the final commit. The history was
scanned for credential-shaped filenames and diff content before publication, and
the scanner was verified against a planted fake `.env` first — a scan that has
never been shown to fire is not evidence of anything.

---

## Reproducing

```bash
python scripts/temp_guard.py                       # verify determinism inside the container
python scripts/calibrate_instrument.py --variant C3 --packet smoke/p0-E1-packet.txt
python scripts/k_variance.py --variant C3 --packet p0-E1-packet
python scripts/a_variance.py --runs 20 --packet smoke/p0-E1-packet.txt
```

Everything needed is in this repository:

* `patches/mirofish-deterministic-cohort.patch` — unified diff against a vendored
  MiroFish-Offline checkout. **The image must be rebuilt afterwards**; both
  compose files bake the source in at build time.
* `smoke/p0-E1-packet.txt` and `smoke/p0-E4-packet.txt` — the two packets, in
  full. They are synthesised prose about a public event (DeepSeek R1 and the
  2025-01-27 NVDA repricing), not compilations of copyrighted headlines, so they
  are included verbatim rather than as synthetic stand-ins.
* `smoke/calibration/raw-C3-p0-E1-packet-2026-08-02T*.json` — the four B runs'
  raw per-persona interviews, and `a-variance-results.json` — all 40 A runs.

**Use the supplied packets verbatim.** The two here are hand-written and carry an
`OPEN QUESTIONS AT T0` section listing what the market is still debating. The
project's automated packet builder does **not** emit that section, so a packet
generated by it is a structurally different input, and a reproduction attempt
using one is not running this experiment.

We do *not* claim that difference drives abstention. The available comparison —
81.8% abstention on a hand-written packet versus 90.0%/96.9% on auto-built ones —
is confounded by questionnaire version, persona count, and event, and was already
recorded as "a hint, not a measurement" before this result existed. All four B
runs used one packet, so none of this affects the finding. It affects whether you
are reproducing it.

## Method notes worth stealing

Independent of the finding, these were what made it trustworthy:

* Every decision rule was written and committed **before** the data it governs —
  nine times, each its own commit, each checkable in the log:

  | commit | what was pinned, before what |
  |---|---|
  | `e7ba7ab` | blind re-grading protocol, before any score was seen |
  | `23dc34a` | regrade protocol, before any scores existed |
  | `b72309b` | retro-eligibility rule, before inspecting any packet |
  | `4db6ca8` | instrument variant selection rule, before any variant ran |
  | `c66fade` | C1/C2/C3 decision rule, before running them |
  | `5499398` | variance rule + crowd determinisation, before running |
  | `181fe1d` | 4-run allocation and patch form, before the runs |
  | `5aacd29` | the D₂ formula, before the 4 runs |
  | `2a6a0aa` | A-arm criteria and both bias corrections, before the 20 runs |

  Two further rule-writes are labelled **post-hoc** because they are, and are not
  counted above: `e774aea` (the E4 generality check, prompted by the E1 result)
  and `78621ec` (the metric correction, written when its approximate magnitude
  was already known by hand).

  A reader grepping this repository will find **13** hashes cited, not nine. The
  other four are the two post-hoc registrations above plus two cited for
  unrelated reasons. All thirteen are listed with timestamps and classification
  in `protocol/pre-registration-manifest.md`, so the count can be checked rather
  than taken on trust.
* Quality gates are **code, not intention**: the analysis record has a hard field
  schema that cannot carry an outcome-bearing column; the adaptive gate raises
  `ResultLeakError` if handed a record containing an outcome; the temperature
  gate fails **closed**, treating "could not verify" exactly like "verified bad".
* Artefact writes **refuse to overwrite**. This was added after the same
  overwrite bug destroyed two successful runs and then, separately, one run's
  raw interviews permanently.
* One bug in the analysis was found *after* the numbers were on screen (the first
  version pooled a pre-patch run into the decision set). The conclusion did not
  change, but the ordering is recorded here because nobody else could have known.
* **A pre-registered prediction was refuted by the data, and the wrong prediction
  is still in the record.** When the metric correction was registered (`78621ec`)
  it stated that weighting B by its conviction field would *increase* B's
  dispersion, making the A-only correction conservative. It *decreased* it,
  0.5879 → 0.3822, and the claim of conservatism was wrong. This matters more
  than the count of pre-registrations above: nine rule-writes can be a ritual,
  but a ritual never leaves behind a record of its own prediction failing.
* **A guard failed open, and finding out why took reproducing it exactly.**
  The pre-commit hook enforcing the append-only ledger printed its refusal and
  the commit landed anyway, deleting all 69 rows. Two attempts to reproduce it
  failed — because both redirected the output, and the redirect removes the
  condition. With the byte-for-byte original command
  (`git commit ... 2>&1 | head -20`, no redirect) it reproduced on the first try.

  The trigger is a **race**, not output volume. Controls: one burst of 30 lines
  blocks; two bursts with no gap block; forty separate `echo`s block; two bursts
  with a 0.2 s gap **fail open**; a subprocess pipeline followed by more output
  **fails open**. What kills the hook is a write issued *after* the reader has
  actually exited — writes faster than `head` can quit all land in the pipe
  buffer. Large output fails open only because filling the buffer stalls the
  writer long enough for the reader to leave: the same race by another road. The
  real hook had the losing shape naturally — `git diff | grep | grep | head` is
  slow, and three `echo`s followed it — which is why 8441 bytes sufficed.

  **The first fix was insufficient and this is worth more than the bug.** Routing
  diagnostics to stderr passed every check that had been written, because the
  refusal was shorter than the reader's limit so the reader never quit early.
  Against `head -3` it failed open again. The fix that holds is `trap '' PIPE`:
  the failed write returns EPIPE instead of killing the shell, so control always
  reaches the exit status. Verified against readers `head -20 / -3 / -1`, with
  and without the trap.

  The independent byte-level check in `tests/test_ledger_integrity.py` was kept
  regardless — two guards that fail in different ways is the whole idea.

* **A verdict was demoted rather than banked.** The corrected A value passes its
  pre-registered threshold — by 2.3×10⁻⁵, against a metric whose own step is
  0.041. Read literally the rule was satisfied; the margin was not meaningful, so
  the claim was downgraded to a descriptive observation and the bands were left
  alone. The easy move was available and is visible in the git history as not
  taken.
